title: The Anointing, the King's Entry, and the Hour
summary: Six days before Passover Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly perfume, and Jesus defends her against Judas, saying she has kept it for his burial. The next day crowds welcome him into Jerusalem with palm branches as the King of Israel, and when some Greeks ask to see him, Jesus announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified, like a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit. The chapter closes John's account of Jesus' public ministry with a reflection on unbelief, drawn from Isaiah, and Jesus' final public appeal.
story: Chapter 12 is the bridge between the two halves of John's Gospel. The first half, often called the Book of Signs, has shown Jesus revealing himself through seven signs and discourses; the second, often called the Book of Glory, will tell of his last evening with the disciples, his death, and his resurrection. Throughout the first half Jesus has said his hour had not yet come. Now, when Greeks come seeking him, he says “The hour has come” (12:23). The raising of Lazarus has brought crowds and sealed the authorities' decision, and the chapter shows both responses side by side: extravagant love and royal welcome on one side, calculation, betrayal, and unbelief on the other.
historical:
The final Passover is approaching, and Jerusalem is filling with pilgrims from across the Jewish world. Estimates of Jerusalem's Passover crowds vary widely, but the city's population swelled many times over. Roman governors usually came up to Jerusalem from Caesarea for the feast with extra troops, since the festival of liberation from Egypt could stir hopes of liberation from Rome. A crowd hailing a man as King of Israel was politically dangerous, which helps explain the authorities' alarm (12:19; see 11:48).

Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory; 1 Maccabees 13:51 records Jews entering Jerusalem with palm branches after Simon Maccabeus's victory in 141 BC. The Greeks of 12:20 were probably Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel without becoming Jews, sometimes called God-fearers, who could pray in the temple's outer court. The chapter notes that many leaders believed but feared being put out of the synagogue (12:42), which shows that the authorities were themselves divided, and that it was the fear of a few that silenced many. Here, as throughout John, the crowd of Jews includes many who believe (12:11), which should keep any reader from treating the Jewish people as Jesus' enemies.
cultural:
Anointing a guest's head with oil was a gesture of honor, but anointing the feet was unusual and humble, and letting down her hair in the presence of men would have been striking for a respectable woman. Nard was an aromatic oil made from a plant that grew in the Himalayan region, imported at great cost. Three hundred denarii would have been about a year's wages for a laborer. Anointing a body for burial with spices and oils was a normal Jewish practice, which is why Jesus interprets the act as preparation for his burial.

The crowd's cry of “Hosanna” comes from Psalm 118:25-26, where the Hebrew means save, we pray. Psalm 118 was part of the Hallel, a group of psalms (113 to 118) sung at the great festivals, so pilgrims knew it by heart. By riding a young donkey Jesus acts out Zechariah 9:9, where Zion's king comes humble and mounted on a donkey rather than a war horse. The image of a seed dying in the ground to bear grain would have been familiar to any farming people.
literary: The chapter has three scenes and two closing reflections. The anointing (12:1-11) and the entry (12:12-19) are both royal acts, since kings were anointed and welcomed in procession, but one points to burial and the other to a humble king. The coming of the Greeks (12:20-36) triggers the turning point of the Gospel, marked by the word hour and by Jesus' troubled prayer, which reads like John's counterpart to Gethsemane in the other Gospels. The narrator's reflection on unbelief (12:37-43) quotes Isaiah 53:1 and Isaiah 6:10, and Jesus' last public words (12:44-50) gather up the themes of the whole first half: belief, sending, light, judgment, and life. John notes twice that the disciples understood only later (12:16), a reminder that the Gospel is written from the far side of Easter.

outline.t: The Greeks come; the grain of wheat
The troubled soul and the voice from heaven
Unbelief and the prophecy of Isaiah

doctrines.note: “Unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed” (12:24). Jesus' death is the way to a harvest of life for many, including the nations. When he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself (12:32), and the ruler of this world will be cast out (12:31).
The crowd hails Jesus as King of Israel, and he accepts it, but he enters as Zechariah's humble king on a donkey. His kingship will be revealed on a cross, under a sign that names him King (19:19).

John says of the unbelievers that “they were unable to believe” and cites Isaiah's words about blinded eyes (12:39-40), while also holding them responsible and describing leaders who did believe but would not confess. See the hard question.
The arrival of the Greeks signals that Jesus' death will open the way for the nations. The Pharisees' complaint that the whole world has gone after him (12:19) is truer than they know.

words.note: Doxazō, to glorify, to give or reveal glory. In John, Jesus is glorified above all in his death, resurrection, and return to the Father. The Son of Man is glorified at the hour of the cross (12:23), which turns the world's idea of glory upside down: the place of shame becomes the place where God's glory is revealed.

Hupsoō, to lift up or exalt. John uses it with a double meaning. Jesus will be lifted up physically on the cross, which is why John adds that he was indicating the kind of death he would die (12:33), and he will be lifted up in exaltation. Isaiah 52:13 in the Greek Old Testament uses this verb for the servant who will be lifted up and glorified.

Pōroō, to harden. Used in the Isaiah quotation (12:40), it describes hearts made dull and unresponsive. In Isaiah 6 the prophet's message would harden those who refused it, and John sees the same pattern in the response to Jesus.

Entaphiasmos, preparation for burial. Jesus says Mary kept the perfume for the day of his burial (12:7). The word shows that Jesus reads her act in light of his coming death, even if she did not fully understand it herself.

christ: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the king Zechariah promised, humble and bringing salvation, and the crowd sings Psalm 118 over him. But the chapter shows that his kingship comes through death. He is the grain of wheat that falls into the ground; the Son of Man lifted up; the servant of Isaiah 53, whose message was not believed. John adds that Isaiah “saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him” (12:41), which links Isaiah's vision of the Lord high and lifted up in the temple (Isaiah 6) with Jesus. John's point is that the glory of the God of Israel is seen in Jesus. His troubled soul (12:27) shows that he goes to the cross as a real man, afraid, and yet willing.

hard.q: If God blinded their eyes so that they could not believe, how can they be blamed?
hard.a:
John quotes Isaiah 6:10 to explain why so many who saw Jesus' signs didn't believe, and says “For this reason they were unable to believe” (12:39). Taken alone, this sounds as though God prevented them. Interpreters have read it in several ways. Augustinian and Reformed readers see here God's sovereign judgment, in which God hands people over to the hardness they have chosen, while still holding them responsible. Others stress that in Isaiah the hardening comes as a judgment after long refusal and that the message itself hardens those who resist it, so the inability is a result of prior unwillingness. Many point out that John's main concern is not to explain human psychology but to reassure his readers that the widespread rejection of Jesus didn't take God by surprise; Scripture had foreseen it.

John himself doesn't resolve the tension, and he immediately adds that many leaders did believe (12:42) and that Jesus continued to plead with people to believe (12:44-50). The chapter holds God's purpose and human responsibility together, as the Bible does elsewhere, without explaining exactly how they fit.

questions: Judas calls Mary's gift a waste. What would it look like for your love for Jesus to seem extravagant to others?
Jesus says whoever loves his life will lose it. What in your life might need to fall into the ground and die so that something can bear fruit?
Some leaders believed but kept quiet because they loved human praise. Where does the desire for approval shape what you are willing to say about your faith?
